title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate
claim: A capable agent needs interacting components: a predictive model, persistent memory, and intrinsic-reward-driven action selection, closed in a loop with the environment.
layout: Single panel, boxes and arrows, nested dashed boundaries, robot cartoon at left
description: A single block diagram with a line-art cartoon robot at the lower left. A large dashed box labeled 'Agent System S = {π, M, P, p_θ}' holds an 'Action Selection (π)' box on the left and a solid inner box labeled 'Curiosity Mechanism (Predictive Component)' on the right. The inner box contains the 'M Prediction' box, a stack of layered panes, a row of filled and empty memory cells, and a cylinder labeled P. Arrows carry 'Prediction Target' from π to M and 'Intrinsic Reward' back from M to π. An 'Update' arc loops over M. 'Persist' and 'Retrieve' arrows connect M and P. A circular 'LLM' node links to the other parts with dotted lines. An 'Environment' bar sits below, joined by 'Action' and 'Observation' arrows. The drawing is monochrome black and white.
caption: Design of conceptual components for a curious agent system S = ⟨pθ, M, P, π⟩. The predictive component M targets environment responses [C1] and updates from observations [C2]; its predicted improvement supplies the intrinsic reward shaping action selection through π [C3]; persistent state P retains improvements beyond the context window [C4]. In open-ended settings, it can also design its own prediction targets and environments [C5].
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.
